title: Realistic Idealism
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that teacher burnout comes less from policies, evaluation rubrics or difficult classes than from the unrealistic expectations teachers carry into each school year. He separates two kinds of expectation: worthy ideals (that small lessons can shift a student's trajectory, that the work aims at long-term flourishing, that we will improve) and impossible ones (that everything will go as planned, that every paper must be graded and read, that the whole to-do list must be done). The ideals protect against burnout and should be held tightly, while the unrealistic expectations must be killed early. He calls the combination realistic idealism and says many of the best career teachers possess it. It requires ignoring both pessimistic voices and the overly optimistic voices that say we can do All The Things. The closing Everest image makes the point that a climber can bring only what is required.
points: Burnout is traced to the teacher's own unrealistic expectations rather than to external policy pressure.
Big-picture ideals such as long-term flourishing of students act as a charm against burnout rather than a cause of it.
Pragmatic grading, whole-class feedback and ruthless triage of pointless tasks are presented as marks of the best career teachers.
Realistic idealism requires resisting two sets of voices at once, the pessimists and the do-everything optimists.
quotes: In my experience, these things create challenging circumstances (and many times the challenge lies not in the things but in the ignoring of them), but they don't burn me out. Really, what burns me out is my unrealistic expectations.
This kind of idealism doesn't lead to burnout; rather, it acts as a charm for keeping burnout at bay.
I have to grade everything, and all of that grading has to be done the same way (when, in fact, some of the best teachers grade very pragmatically);
What I've briefly painted here is what many of the best career teachers possess: realistic idealism. That first set of bullet points is about as high-minded as it comes. It is hugely idealistic.
But that bottom list is interesting because, to hold to it, we need to ignore the overly optimistic voices that surround us — those who believe that we can somehow do All The Things.
You can't climb up Mount Everest with your kitchen sink. You can bring only what is required.
